narrative: In the same month, two security researchers independently discovered a serious authentication bypass vulnerability in a major financial services platform used by tens of thousands of small business customers across Europe. The vulnerability allowed any authenticated user to access any other customer's account by manipulating a session token in a predictable way. Both researchers found it while testing their own accounts on the platform. Neither had been hired to test anything.

Priya Mehta, the first researcher, documented the vulnerability carefully, photographed the proof-of-concept, and immediately closed her browser. She then searched the company's website for a responsible disclosure policy. Finding none, she sent an email to the company's general security contact address, describing the vulnerability in technical detail, including the proof-of-concept, and stating clearly that she had not accessed any accounts other than her own. She requested acknowledgement within five business days and stated she would follow a 90-day disclosure timeline — giving the company ninety days to release a patch before she published her findings.

Marcus Webb, the second researcher, accessed his own account to confirm the vulnerability, then accessed three other accounts to 'verify it worked across different customer types.' He published a detailed blog post with full proof-of-concept code that same evening, before contacting the company. He tagged the company in his social media post. The post went viral within twelve hours.

The company's legal team contacted Priya within twenty-four hours. After an initially tense exchange, they established a working relationship. Priya received a formal letter of thanks, a £2,500 bug bounty payment under an emergency programme they established specifically to handle her submission, and a reference for her professional portfolio. The vulnerability was patched in eighteen days. Priya's name appeared in the company's security acknowledgements page.

Marcus received a letter from the company's lawyers. He had accessed accounts he was not authorised to access — that constituted unauthorised computer access under the Computer Misuse Act regardless of his purpose. He had caused the company measurable reputational damage by going public before a patch was available. The criminal referral was ultimately dropped after Marcus agreed to remove the post and cooperate with the investigation — but the legal process took eleven months, cost him significant money in legal fees, and ended his career at his employer, who terminated him during the investigation.

characters.name: Priya Mehta
characters.description: A developer who discovered a critical vulnerability while using a platform for her own business. Her disciplined approach to responsible disclosure — limit access to her own account, contact the company privately, set a professional timeline — turned an accidental discovery into a career milestone.

characters.name: Marcus Webb
characters.description: A technically skilled developer whose discovery was equally valid — but whose actions after the discovery turned a potential career highlight into an eleven-month legal ordeal. He accessed accounts he was not authorised to access and published a working exploit before giving the company any opportunity to respond.
